chunks.arabic_text: اَلْكَافِّي: عَلِيُّ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ، عَنْ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ صَالِحٍ قَالَ

translations.en: Al-Kafi: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Salih who said:

chunks.arabic_text: لَمَّا مَاتَ أَبِي وَصَارَ الْأَمْرُ لِي، كَانَ لِيَ عَلَى النَّاسِ سَفَاتِجُ مِنْ مَالِ الْغَرِيمِ، فَكَتَبْتُ إِلَيْهِ أَعْلِمُهُ، فَكَتَبَ: طَالِبَهُمْ وَاسْتَقْضِ عَلَيْهِمْ، فَقَضَانِيَ النَّاسُ إِلَّا رَجُلًا وَاحِدًا كَانَتْ عَلَيْهِ سِفْتَجَةٌ بِأَرْبَعِمِائَةِ دِينَارٍ، فَجِئْتُ إِلَيْهِ أَطْلُبُهُ فَمَاطَلَنِي وَاسْتَخَفَّ بِي ابْنُهُ وَسَفِهَ عَلَيَّ، فَشَكَوْتُ إِلَى أَبِيهِ فَقَالَ: وَكَانَ مَاذَا؟ فَقَبَضْتُ عَلَى لِحْيَتِهِ وَأَخَذْتُ بِرِجْلِهِ وَسَحَبْتُهُ إِلَى وَسَطِ الدَّارِ وَرَكَلْتُهُ رَكْلًا كَثِيرًا، فَخَرَجَ ابْنُهُ يَسْتَغِيثُ بِأَهْلِ بَغْدَانَ وَيَقُولُ: قُمِّي رَافِضِيٌّ قَدْ قَلَى وَالِدِي، فَاجْتَمَعَ عَلَيَّ مِنْهُمُ الْخَلْقُ، فَرَكِبْتُ دَابَّتِي وَقُلْتُ: أَحْسَنْتُمْ يَا أَهْلَ بَغْدَانَ تَمِيلُونَ مَعَ الظَّالِمِ عَلَى الْغَرِيبِ الْمَظْلُومِ، أَنَا رَجُلٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ هَمْدَانَ مِنْ أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ، وَهَذَا يَنْسُبُنِي إِلَى أَهْلِ قُمَّ وَالرَّفْضِ لِيَذْهَبَ بِحَقِّي وَمَالِي، قَالَ: فَمَالُوا عَلَيْهِ وَأَرَادُوا أَنْ يَدْخُلُوا عَلَى حَانُوتِهِ حَتَّى سَكَّنَتْهُمْ وَطَلَبَ إِلَيَّ صَاحِبُ السِّفْتَجَةِ وَحَلَفَ بِالطَّلَاقِ أَنْ يُوفِينِي مَالِي حَتَّى أَخْرَجْتُهُ عَنْهُ

translations.en: When my father died and the matter devolved to me, I had bills of exchange from the wealth of the Creditor (the Imam) against the people. I wrote to him to inform him, and he wrote back: 'Seek them out and demand payment from them.' The people paid me except for one man who had a bill of four hundred dinars. I went to him to demand it, but he delayed me, and his son made light of me and ridiculed me. I complained to his father, and he said: 'What happened?' So I grabbed his beard, took hold of his leg, dragged him to the middle of the house, and kicked him many times. His son came out shouting for help from the people of Baghdad, saying: 'A Qummi Rafidhi has killed my father!' A crowd gathered around me, so I mounted my horse and said: 'Well done, O people of Baghdad! You side with the oppressor against the oppressed stranger. I am a man from the people of Hamadan, from the Ahl al-Sunnah, and this man is ascribing me to the people of Qum and Rafdh to take away my right and wealth.' He said: 'They turned against him and wanted to enter his shop until I quieted them down. The man whose bill it was sought me out and swore by divorce that he would pay me my money if I would take them away from him.'

en.summary: This narrative from al-Kafi illustrates the practical authority of the Imam’s representative (Wakil) in civil matters, specifically debt collection, highlighting the interplay between legal entitlement and social dynamics in Abbasid Baghdad. Muhammad ibn Salih’s strategic use of physical confrontation and rhetorical framing—portraying himself as a Sunni outsider to counter the 'Rafidi' label of the debtor’s son—demonstrates how early Shia scholars navigated sectarian tensions to assert their rights. The incident underscores the Wali’s role not just as a spiritual guide but as an active agent in enforcing financial obligations within the community.
en.seo_question: How did the Imam's representative collect a difficult debt in Baghdad?

key_terms.سَفَاتِجُ: Bills of exchange or promissory notes
key_terms.سِفْتَجَةٌ: A bill or note of debt
key_terms.أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ: People of the Sunnah (referring to the Sunni majority)
key_terms.الرَّفْضِ: Rafdh (a term for Shia, often used pejoratively by Sunnis)
